title: Make a moka pot ready to brew: fill the base to just below the safety valve and screw the top on snug
instruction: Get the moka pot ready to brew.
context: Baristas and cooks (O*NET 35-3023.01, Baristas; 35-2014.00, Cooks, Restaurant), and anyone making coffee at home on a stovetop moka pot, fill its base with water up to just below the brass safety valve and then screw the upper chamber on snug before it goes on the heat. Over the valve, the valve stands in water and cannot vent steam if the coffee clogs the funnel, so the pot can over-pressure; more than about 1 cm under it, too little water makes weak, under-extracted coffee; a top that is loose or on crooked leaks steam and hot coffee at the gasket. The base is already on the cold burner, and the carafe holds more water than the base should take, so emptying it in, or setting the top on without screwing it tight, are the tempting wrong answers.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0, all at real size. A stainless steel hob plate 14 x 14 x 0.4 cm with a black burner cap 5.6 cm across is fixed centered at (27, 5), with a cast-iron grate on it: four diagonal fingers 1.2 cm wide and 1.4 cm tall from 2.2 to 6.6 cm off the burner's axis and a ring 13.2 cm across. The empty base (water chamber) of a 3-cup cast-aluminum moka pot stands on the grate, fixed there (a real cook steadies it with the other hand), axis at (27, 5), foot at z 1.8: 7.2 cm tall, 8.2 cm across at the foot tapering to a threaded collar 6.6 cm across (its top 1.2 cm); inside it steps from 7.2 to 6.6 to 6.2 cm across, floor 4 mm above the foot, steps 2.4 and 4.4 cm above the foot. Its brass safety valve (hex 1.3 cm across, with a pin) faces the robot (-x), its center 5.0 cm above the foot; the valve's 8 mm bore shows as a brass ring inside the wall, its bottom edge 4.6 cm above the foot (155.8 mL of water). The upper chamber (aluminum, 200 g, free) stands upright on the counter at (24, 19): 8.7 cm tall, 7.0 cm across on its lower body and 8.0 cm at the top, with a lid knob, a small spout and a black plastic handle pointing 45 degrees off the x axis, and a skirt (female thread) 1.2 cm deep under it, which goes over the base's collar; eight round ribs inside the skirt keep it within 2 mm of the collar's axis once it is down over it. Assembled the pot is 15.9 cm tall. A glass carafe (cylinder 4.9 cm across, 13.5 cm tall, 4.4 cm inside, 200 g) holding 175 mL of water stands at (23, -12). The water is drawn as a blue column inside each vessel.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run and scores the end state. 0: more than 155.8 mL in the base (above the bottom of the valve bore) or under 30 mL (includes doing nothing). 0.25: 30 to 122.5 mL (more than 1 cm under the valve: weak coffee) with the top screwed snug, or 122.5 to 155.8 mL with the upper chamber not screwed snug; a short pour with the top not screwed snug either is 0. On the base: its bottom face within 4 mm of the rim height, its axis within 4 mm and 4 degrees of the base's (more is cross-threaded). Screwed snug: on the base and turned clockwise (seen from above) 450 to 720 degrees since it went on, counting only turning done while a gripper's fingers are closed on it (stopped by its 7 cm body, tool point within 1.5 cm of its axis) and only up to 1.25 times that gripper's own wrist roll in the same direction, so a swipe by the other arm, a resting or wiggling hand earns nothing; any counterclockwise turning counts against it and lifting it off the collar restarts the count. 450 degrees is a 3-cup pot's 1.25 turns from catch to gasket; past 2 turns a real thread has stopped, so a top still turning was not biting. 0.5: filled and screwed, but over 5 mL spilled, the carafe not set down upright, let go and off the stove, the base tipped over 10 degrees or moved over 2 cm off the burner, or a closed hand still on the upper chamber (gripping any part of its side, or within 1.5 cm of it or its lid knob). 1.0: all of it with both arms back within 3 cm of their start and still; 0.9 with an arm not home. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1. A real trial weighs the water in the base before the top goes on (or reads it against the valve bore from above, as the camera does), checks by hand that the top will not turn further without force and does not lift, and weighs a towel under the hob for spills.
reset_notes: Empty and dry the base and stand it on the grate with the valve toward the robot; unscrew the upper chamber and stand it upright at (24, 19) with its handle 45 degrees off the x axis; refill the carafe to 175 mL with a measuring jug and stand it at (23, -12); replace the towel under the hob. The burner stays off and cold.
fidelity: Real size, no fluid simulation: the water is a deterministic flow model pouring into the opening below a tipped carafe's lip, or onto the table as spill. No physical thread: the upper chamber is a free body that drops over the base's collar and screwing is scored from its gripped turning there, with no torque rise at snug. The base is fixed on the grate (a cook steadies it by hand); no heat or steam; the funnel basket step is cut.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps; it never touched the carafe or the pot); demo: 1.0 (1,730 steps)
